A gravitational-wave signal is an observation of a source, not a direct description of it.

Different combinations of source parameters can sometimes produce very similar observed signals.

That makes gravitational-wave inference an inverse problem: we observe the waveform and try to infer the system that produced it.

## The basic idea

Suppose we observe a reference waveform.

We then vary two source parameters and compare the resulting candidate waveform with the reference.

Some combinations may look noticeably different.

Others may be surprisingly similar.

## A degeneracy

If many different parameter combinations produce nearly the same observation, the inverse problem does not have one obvious answer.

Instead, there can be a region of parameter space where many solutions are plausible.

That structure is often described as a parameter degeneracy.

## Why this matters for machine learning

A model can only infer what is present in the data.

If two physically different systems produce almost indistinguishable observations, a more complicated model does not automatically solve the problem.

The ambiguity is partly in the data itself.

## Breaking the degeneracy

More information can help.

Longer observations, additional waveform structure or richer detector information may distinguish systems that initially looked equivalent.

The interesting question is therefore not only:

**What can the model learn?**

but also:

**What does the observation make possible to learn in the first place?**
